sections.heading: What is Binary Search on Answer?
sections.content: Instead of searching for a value inside an array, you binary search over the range of possible answers. You guess a value, run a quick check function (is this answer feasible?), and move left or right depending on the result. It works when feasibility is monotonic: once an answer is feasible, every larger (or every smaller) answer is also feasible. The total cost is O(log(range) * cost of the check).

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: The problem asks to minimize the maximum or maximize the minimum
You can quickly check whether a given answer works (a yes/no test)
The answer lies in a numeric range with clear lower and upper bounds
If answer x works, then x + 1 (or x - 1) also works
Keywords: minimum time, smallest capacity, largest minimum distance, at most K days, split array
Brute forcing every possible answer is too slow

sections.heading: The Core Idea
sections.content: Imagine the answers laid out in a line: false, false, false, true, true, true. The check function tells you whether each candidate is feasible. Binary search finds the first true (for minimizing) or the last true (for maximizing). You never need the array to be sorted, only the feasibility to flip once.

rows.search: If feasible(mid) then right = mid, else left = mid + 1
If feasible(mid) then left = mid, else right = mid - 1

sections.heading: Template 1: Minimize (Find First True)
Template 2: Maximize (Find Last True)
Step-by-Step Recipe
items: 1. Define what the answer is (time, speed, capacity, distance, size)
2. Find the lowest possible answer (low) and the highest possible answer (high)
3. Write isFeasible(x): can the task be done with this answer?
4. Check monotonicity: if x works, does every larger (or smaller) value work?
5. Pick the minimize or maximize template
6. Use Long if values or sums can exceed Int

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Using the minimize template (mid rounded down) for a maximize problem, which loops forever; round mid up
Setting low or high wrongly (for example low = 0 when the answer must be at least the max element)
A check function that is not monotonic, which breaks binary search
Integer overflow in sums and ceil divisions; use Long
Using a comparison that is off by one: <= versus < in the feasibility test
Forgetting that ceil(a / b) in integers is (a + b - 1) / b
Using left < right style with doubles; use a fixed number of iterations instead
Forgetting to sort first in placement problems such as aggressive cows

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Binary search works on any monotonic yes/no condition, not only sorted arrays
Define low, high and a feasibility check, then pick the right template
Minimize uses right = mid and rounds mid down; maximize uses left = mid and rounds mid up
Most feasibility checks are a single greedy O(n) pass
Use Long for large sums and (a + b - 1) / b for integer ceiling
Total time is O(n log(range)), far faster than trying every answer
